A worked research memo

Compare after drafting your own attempt. This example deliberately reveals evaluation evidence; record that exposure in any later plan. The 692-word memo below is a study example, not independent assessment evidence. Rubric annotations sit outside the memo word count.

Read the worked memo and its results

My question is whether the fixed three-close rule improves the observed trade-off against a matching net buy-and-hold benchmark. I do not find convincing evidence of improvement in this small teaching example. At the base cost, strategy wealth ends at £917.91, compared with benchmark wealth of £978.24, from the same £1,000 initial capital. This is a conditional description of a supplied scenario, not evidence that the rule will succeed or fail in a real market.

The source is the original synthetic dataset qf-synthetic-evaluation-2026-v1, supplied with Chapter 10. It contains invented daily opens and closes, not historical security prices. I used the complete supplied evaluation segment and retained its original row order. The input CSV and accompanying evidence file identify every observation. I have already inspected this public worked example, so I cannot describe a later reproduction as a genuinely unseen test. That exposure matters more than calling the segment “evaluation.”

The rule holds the asset when its latest close exceeds the trailing mean of three closes; otherwise it holds cash. The signal becomes available only after the close. Any resulting trade occurs at the next eligible open. For example, the February 3 close of 107 exceeds the mean of 101, 102 and 107, or 103.333333. The resulting entry uses the February 4 open of 101. Applying that signal to an earlier open would use unavailable information and invalidate the comparison.

I fixed the window at three closes and compared two declared cost cases, 10 and 30 basis points per unit of traded notional. Entry, position switches and final liquidation incur costs; the matching benchmark also pays its entry and exit costs. Cash earns zero. There are no deposits, withdrawals, taxes or additional slippage. Both approaches use the same eligible entry and final exit dates. I retained both cases rather than reporting whichever one appeared more attractive, and did not search alternative windows.

As an independent arithmetic check, the first strategy interval starts with £1,000, pays an entry factor of 0.999 and experiences the open-to-open price factor 97/101. Thus 1000 × 0.999 × 97/101 = £959.435644, matching the first row of the base ledger before rounding. The following row accounts for the move back to cash. For reproduction, use the supplied CSV, freeze the declared inputs, run both cases and compare the complete rows in the attached evidence; matching only a headline is insufficient.

The base strategy total return is -8.21%; the matching benchmark return is -2.18%. At 30 basis points, final strategy wealth is £910.58 and benchmark wealth is £974.33. These amounts include final liquidation. Higher assumed costs reduce wealth in this experiment. The sensitivity is a comparison under a second assumption, not an estimate of the probability of those costs or a correction for every real trading friction.

Risk also needs an explicit convention. Maximum drawdown is the positive magnitude of the largest decline from running peak wealth, including initial capital, observed interval endpoints and final liquidation. Base strategy drawdown is 8.21% and benchmark drawdown is 9.80%. I have not annualised these short-sample results or treated them as future loss bounds. Endpoint observations can miss losses within an interval; a similar ending value would not imply an identical path or risk experience.

Three limitations materially restrict the decision. First, invented prices cannot establish investability, market representativeness or future performance. Second, a tiny sequence provides weak evidence about stability across economic conditions. Third, assumed costs, zero cash return and omitted slippage or taxes can change a comparison. Public inspection also prevents independent validation claims. My next research step would specify new evidence and realistic assumptions before examining outcomes, retain every trial and document deviations; this exercise alone does not justify deploying capital.

In revision, I replaced “the backtest proves the strategy is safe” with “the observed drawdown is conditional on these synthetic rows and declared costs.” That correction addresses interpretation and traceability: it names the observation basis and removes an unsupported guarantee. I also checked the headline amounts against the exported ledger and retained the unfavourable strategy result. The memo and rubric annotations support learner self-review; neither a word count nor an automated calculation check independently validates the reasoning or awards a credential.

Read it against the rubric

Data and reproducibility

Paragraphs 2 and 5 identify synthetic provenance, version, ordered inputs, exposure and reproduction evidence.

Calculations and conventions

Paragraphs 5–7 provide the hand calculation, final wealth, returns, costs and drawdown definition. Recalculate the first interval before comparing.

Timing, benchmark, costs and evaluation design

Paragraphs 3–4 distinguish signal availability from execution and declare matching dates, both cost cases and no window search.

Interpretation and limitations

Paragraphs 1 and 8 make a conditional decision and explain consequential limits, rather than treating a negative result as a failed assignment.

Clarity and response to feedback

Paragraph 9 records a specific unsupported claim, its correction and why the correction improves the reasoning.

The five headings match the chapter rubric. They explain where to look for evidence; they do not award a validated score. Identify a weakness yourself, state the evidence and revise your own memo.
